title: Problem framing
text: Signs: the candidate starts proposing a solution right after hearing the question. They never ask or state who the customer is, what the goal is, or what is in scope, so the rest of the answer rests on hidden assumptions. How to fix: spend the first minute defining the problem. Ask about the goal, the type of customer, and any constraints, or state your assumptions out loud if the interviewer does not answer. For example: "Before designing this, I want to confirm: are we trying to reduce churn or win new accounts, and are we focused on small businesses or enterprise customers?"

title: User segmentation
text: Signs: the candidate talks about "users" or "customers" as if they were one group. They do not say who buys the product, who uses it every day, or which type of company they have in mind, so the solution fits nobody in particular. How to fix: name two or three segments, pick one, and explain why. In B2B, always separate the buyer from the user. For example: "The buyer is the finance director, who cares about cost. The daily user is the warehouse manager, who cares about speed. I'll focus on the warehouse manager, because adoption is where this product fails today."

title: Prioritization
text: Signs: the candidate lists many ideas or features and treats them all as equally important. They never say which one they would build first, or they say the team should do all of them, which avoids the hard decision. How to fix: state clear criteria, compare the options against them, and choose one. Say what you would not do and why. For example: "I see three options. I'd compare them on customer impact, reach, and effort. I'd build the CRM integration first, because it affects the most accounts, and I'd postpone the mobile app until next quarter."

title: Success metrics
text: Signs: the candidate describes a solution in detail but never says how anyone would know it worked. They may say "users will love it" or "it will improve engagement" without naming a number. How to fix: name one metric tied to the goal, say how it is measured, and give a target or a direction, for example "% of managers who log waste weekly, measured over the first 60 days."

title: Tradeoffs and risks
text: Signs: the candidate presents their idea as if it had no downside. They do not mention costs, risks, or alternatives they rejected, and they do not say what the team gives up by choosing this path. How to fix: name at least one real cost or risk of your recommendation and explain why it is still worth it, along with how you would reduce the risk. For example: "Moving upmarket brings larger contracts, but it could pull engineers away from our small business customers. I'd accept that risk by limiting it to a pilot with five enterprise accounts."

title: Business impact
text: Signs: the candidate only discusses features or user experience and never connects them to the company's results. They do not mention revenue, retention, expansion, or why a B2B buyer would pay for this or renew. How to fix: link the proposal to a business outcome and to the person who controls the budget, using a rough estimate when possible. For example: "If faster onboarding raises activation from 40% to 50%, more accounts reach renewal, and that lowers churn. It also gives the buyer a clear return on investment, which supports the renewal conversation."

title: Solution specificity
text: Signs: the candidate names a general idea, such as "add an AI dashboard" or "improve the onboarding", without saying what it actually does. The interviewer could not explain what the team would build, what the user would see, or how it would work. How to fix: describe one specific feature and walk through the user flow step by step. For example: "When a new account signs up, the admin imports employees from a spreadsheet, the system flags missing tax data, and the admin fixes those errors on one screen before the first payroll runs."

title: Structure
text: Signs: the candidate jumps between ideas with no visible order. Users, features, and metrics appear at random, the answer repeats itself, and it is hard to follow where it is going or when it has ended. How to fix: announce a simple plan at the start, follow it, and signal each transition. The framework can be basic, as long as it fits the question. For example: "I'll cover this in four steps: the goal, the customer, the options, and how I'd measure success. Let me start with the goal." Finish with a short summary and a clear conclusion.

title: Staying on topic
text: The answer must address the question asked. An answer about a different problem, or generic career talk that never touches the scenario, is off topic.

title: Minimum substance
text: An empty answer or one with only a few words cannot be assessed and counts as too short.

title: Product strategy questions
text: A strong product strategy answer starts by clarifying the company's objective, such as growth, revenue, retention, or defensibility, before judging any option. It analyzes the market and the competitors, then assesses the company's real advantages and gaps, including distribution, data, ecosystem, and customer trust. In B2B, it segments customers by size and buying process, because small businesses and enterprise accounts need different things. It compares realistic options, then makes one clear recommendation instead of listing possibilities. It names the main risks, including distraction from the core business, and explains how to test the decision, for example with a pilot, before full commitment. It closes with the metrics that would show whether the bet is working.

title: Product sense questions
text: A strong product sense answer starts by clarifying the scope and the goal before proposing anything. It identifies the people involved and, in B2B, separates the buyer who pays from the user who works in the product every day. It picks one segment and one pain point, and it justifies that choice instead of trying to solve everything. It then proposes a concrete solution and walks through the core user flow, including how it fits existing workflows and tools. It defines one success metric tied to the goal, such as time to first value or a reduction in manual work. It finishes by naming a real tradeoff or risk, such as low data quality or resistance from users, and how to handle it.

title: Analytical execution questions
text: A strong analytical execution answer starts with the goal of the product before naming any number. It picks one north-star metric that reflects the value customers get, then adds two or three supporting metrics and one guardrail metric that would warn if the team optimizes the wrong thing. In B2B, it separates the buyer who pays from the user who works in the product every day, because they care about different outcomes. It says how each metric is measured and over what time period, and it explains why it rejected at least one obvious metric. When investigating a metric drop, it confirms the definition and the data, checks external factors, segments by account size, role, and region, and tests hypotheses in order. When reading an A/B test, it checks validity, quantifies the net business impact, and makes a clear decision.

title: Behavioral questions
text: A strong behavioral answer uses a clear structure such as STAR: situation, task, action, and result. It gives brief context and explains the stakes, without spending most of the time on background. It focuses on what the candidate personally did, using "I" rather than "we", and it describes specific actions such as using data, building a prototype, or finding allies. It shows understanding of the other person's incentives and point of view. It ends with a concrete outcome, ideally with a number, and takes ownership of the candidate's part in it without blaming others. It closes by reflecting on what the candidate learned and how they applied that lesson later. A failure story must be a real failure, not a disguised success.

title: Technical fluency questions
text: A strong technical fluency answer explains the concept clearly and accurately, at the level a PM needs, without unnecessary jargon. It adapts the explanation to the audience, using a simple analogy for a non-technical executive. It connects technical concepts to business consequences such as cost, latency, reliability, security, and customer risk. When there are several approaches, it compares them on real tradeoffs like cost, maintenance, and data needs, and then recommends one instead of staying neutral. It treats engineers as partners, seeking to understand what drives an estimate or constraint before pushing back. For AI features, it explains how quality would be evaluated, what guardrails are needed, and when a human should stay in the loop.
